source_user: Give one misleading intuition about pipeline parallelism and correct it. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Pipeline parallelism partitions layers across stages and can require microbatching to reduce pipeline bubbles.
corrected_answer:
Misleading intuition: "pipeline parallelism gives you near-linear speedup once you use enough
microbatches, so PP is a cheap way to scale past one node."

Why it is wrong, concretely:

1. The bubble never reaches zero in a synchronous schedule. Mechanism (must be stated explicitly): with pipeline degree P and M microbatches per global
batch, a synchronous 1F1B schedule has bubble fraction (P-1)/(M+P-1) of the per-stage compute time,
assuming perfectly balanced stages and zero communication cost. Interleaved (virtual pipeline) 1F1B
with v model chunks per device reduces this to (P-1)/(v*M+P-1) at the cost of v times more
stage-boundary point-to-point transfers per step.

Boundary condition (where the formula stops holding): the bubble formula assumes stage compute is
balanced and that the boundary send/recv is fully overlapped. It breaks down when (a) stages are
imbalanced -- the slowest stage sets the step time and the embedding/LM-head stages are the usual
offenders; (b) the stage boundary crosses a node and the activation tensor per microbatch
(micro_bs * S * H * dtype_bytes) exceeds what the measured inter-node RDMA/RoCE bandwidth can move
inside one stage's compute window, at which point you are communication-bound and adding microbatches
stops helping; (c) memory: peak activation memory scales with the number of in-flight microbatches
(~P under 1F1B), so raising M past that point does not raise memory but raising P does.

2. Even in the limit of large M, PP does not add throughput the way data parallelism does -- it lets a
model that does not fit on one device run at all, and it adds per-step point-to-point traffic. With
P=8 and M=8 the bubble alone is 7/15 = 47% of ideal; you need roughly M >= 4P before the bubble drops
under ~6%, and large M inflates the global batch size, which is a training-dynamics change, not a free
knob.

3. The second half of the intuition ("cheap way to scale past one node") is the more dangerous half.
PP is often the right parallelism to place on the slow inter-node link precisely because it sends one
activation tensor per microbatch boundary instead of all-reducing full gradients, but that only holds
while micro_bs*S*H*dtype_bytes divided by measured link bandwidth stays small relative to one stage's
compute time. Cross that ratio and every added microbatch adds exposed communication instead of hiding
bubble.

Corrected statement: PP converts a memory constraint into a latency/bubble constraint. Its ceiling is
set by max(slowest stage, exposed boundary communication), and the term (P-1)/(M+P-1) is a lower bound
on the loss, not an estimate of it.

Falsifiable form: "at P=4, M=32, 1F1B, recomputation off, we retain >=85% of the single-stage per-GPU
TFLOP/s." Falsified if measured per-GPU TFLOP/s ratio < 0.85, or if the profiler shows exposed
send/recv > 5% of step time.

Rollback gate: if end-to-end tokens/s regresses >3% versus the current production parallelism plan, or
if any rank's peak memory exceeds 90% of device memory, revert to the previous (P, TP, M) triple before
the next checkpoint interval. (Case variant 5.)

Treating nameplate NIC bandwidth as achievable inter-stage bandwidth overstates the microbatch count at which PP stays compute-bound
Raising pipeline degree P to fix a memory problem can convert a compute-bound job into a communication-bound one on inter-node boundaries
Changing M changes global batch size, so any convergence claim drawn from a throughput sweep is invalid without LR re-tuning
Source answer states the mechanism as if it were the correction, leaving the misleading near-linear-speedup intuition intact
evidence_required: Per-stage forward/backward wall time from torch profiler or Megatron-LM timers, to prove or disprove stage balance
Measured stage-boundary point-to-point bandwidth (ib_write_bw for RDMA, nccl-tests sendrecv) rather than nameplate NIC speed
Nsight Systems or torch profiler timeline showing actual bubble width vs the (P-1)/(M+P-1) prediction
Recorded config: P, TP, DP, M, micro_bs, schedule (GPipe / 1F1B / interleaved), activation recomputation on-off, dtype
torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated per stage to confirm the in-flight-microbatch memory model
NCCL_DEBUG=INFO transport lines confirming GPUDirect RDMA is active on inter-node boundaries and not silently host-staged

source_user: Design a small controlled experiment for pipeline parallelism. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Pipeline parallelism partitions layers across stages and can require microbatching to reduce pipeline bubbles.
corrected_answer:
Controlled experiment: does increasing microbatch count M actually buy back the pipeline bubble
on this cluster, and where does it stop?

Hypothesis (falsifiable): with stages balanced to within 5%, step time follows
T(M) ~ T_compute * (1 + (P-1)/M) up to the point where exposed stage-boundary communication becomes the
binding term; beyond that, T(M) flattens or worsens.

Mechanism (must be stated explicitly): with pipeline degree P and M microbatches per global
batch, a synchronous 1F1B schedule has bubble fraction (P-1)/(M+P-1) of the per-stage compute time,
assuming perfectly balanced stages and zero communication cost. Interleaved (virtual pipeline) 1F1B
with v model chunks per device reduces this to (P-1)/(v*M+P-1) at the cost of v times more
stage-boundary point-to-point transfers per step.

Boundary condition (where the formula stops holding): the bubble formula assumes stage compute is
balanced and that the boundary send/recv is fully overlapped. It breaks down when (a) stages are
imbalanced -- the slowest stage sets the step time and the embedding/LM-head stages are the usual
offenders; (b) the stage boundary crosses a node and the activation tensor per microbatch
(micro_bs * S * H * dtype_bytes) exceeds what the measured inter-node RDMA/RoCE bandwidth can move
inside one stage's compute window, at which point you are communication-bound and adding microbatches
stops helping; (c) memory: peak activation memory scales with the number of in-flight microbatches
(~P under 1F1B), so raising M past that point does not raise memory but raising P does.

Design:
- Independent variable: M in {P, 2P, 4P, 8P}. Everything else frozen.
- Controls held fixed and recorded: P, TP degree, DP degree, micro_bs, sequence length S, dtype,
  schedule (1F1B), activation recomputation setting, NCCL env (NCCL_ALGO, NCCL_PROTO, NCCL_IB_DISABLE),
  driver/NCCL/framework versions, and which stage boundaries cross a node.
- Arm A: all stage boundaries intra-node (NVLink/PCIe). Arm B: identical config with one boundary forced
  across the RDMA/RoCE fabric. The A-vs-B delta at each M isolates the communication term from the
  bubble term -- a single-arm sweep cannot distinguish a bubble from an exposed send, which is the whole
  reason for the second arm.
- Dependent variables: step time, per-GPU TFLOP/s, exposed send/recv time from the profiler, per-stage
  peak memory.
- Repeats: at least 5 measured steps after at least 20 warmup steps; report median and p90. A single
  step is noise.

Prediction and refutation: if T(M) does not fall roughly as 1/M in Arm A, the stages are imbalanced and
the bubble model is not the limiter -- measure per-stage time before touching M. If Arm B diverges from
Arm A beyond M=4P, you are communication-bound at the node boundary and the fix is to relocate the
boundary or shrink micro_bs*S*H, not to add microbatches.

Confounds to pre-empt: changing M changes global batch size, so loss-curve comparisons across arms are
invalid unless the LR schedule is re-tuned. This experiment measures throughput only; any convergence
claim needs a separate run.

Evidence to capture: Per-stage forward/backward wall time from torch profiler or Megatron-LM timers, to prove or disprove stage balance; Measured stage-boundary point-to-point bandwidth (ib_write_bw for RDMA, nccl-tests sendrecv) rather than nameplate NIC speed; Nsight Systems or torch profiler timeline showing actual bubble width vs the (P-1)/(M+P-1) prediction; Recorded config: P, TP, DP, M, micro_bs, schedule (GPipe / 1F1B / interleaved), activation recomputation on-off, dtype; torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated per stage to confirm the in-flight-microbatch memory model; NCCL_DEBUG=INFO transport lines confirming GPUDirect RDMA is active on inter-node boundaries and not silently host-staged.

Rollback gate: this runs as a scratch benchmark job, not a production config change. Promote a winning
(P, M) only after a full-scale run holds a >=3% throughput gain with no per-stage peak memory above 90%
and no loss-curve deviation beyond the established seed-noise band; otherwise revert. (Case variant 1.)

source_assistant: Pipeline parallelism partitions layers across stages and can require microbatching to reduce pipeline bubbles.
corrected_answer:
Runbook entry: pipeline-parallel throughput or OOM investigation.

Precondition: read-only triage first. Do not change P, M, or the recomputation flag on a running
production job before step 6.

Step 1 -- pin the config. Record P, TP, DP, ZeRO stage, M, micro_bs, S, dtype, schedule
(GPipe / 1F1B / interleaved-1F1B with v chunks), activation recomputation on/off, and the rank-to-node
map. A throughput number without these is not comparable to any other number.

Step 2 -- separate a bubble problem from a balance problem. Mechanism (must be stated explicitly): with pipeline degree P and M microbatches per global
batch, a synchronous 1F1B schedule has bubble fraction (P-1)/(M+P-1) of the per-stage compute time,
assuming perfectly balanced stages and zero communication cost. Interleaved (virtual pipeline) 1F1B
with v model chunks per device reduces this to (P-1)/(v*M+P-1) at the cost of v times more
stage-boundary point-to-point transfers per step.

Boundary condition (where the formula stops holding): the bubble formula assumes stage compute is
balanced and that the boundary send/recv is fully overlapped. It breaks down when (a) stages are
imbalanced -- the slowest stage sets the step time and the embedding/LM-head stages are the usual
offenders; (b) the stage boundary crosses a node and the activation tensor per microbatch
(micro_bs * S * H * dtype_bytes) exceeds what the measured inter-node RDMA/RoCE bandwidth can move
inside one stage's compute window, at which point you are communication-bound and adding microbatches
stops helping; (c) memory: peak activation memory scales with the number of in-flight microbatches
(~P under 1F1B), so raising M past that point does not raise memory but raising P does.
Compute the predicted bubble (P-1)/(M+P-1) and compare it with the measured idle fraction. If the
measured loss far exceeds the prediction, the cause is imbalance or exposed communication, not the
bubble.

Step 3 -- check stage balance. Pull per-stage forward/backward timers. The first stage (embedding) and
last stage (LM head plus loss) are the usual outliers; a spread above 10% means rebalance the layer
assignment before touching anything else. Rebalancing is usually the largest single win and costs no
memory.

Step 4 -- check the boundary link. For every stage boundary that crosses a node, measure actual
bandwidth (ib_write_bw, nccl-tests sendrecv), not the nameplate. Compare
micro_bs*S*H*dtype_bytes / measured_BW against one stage's compute time. If that ratio is not well
below 1, you are communication-bound: adding microbatches will not help. Correct moves are to relocate
the boundary inside a node, reduce micro_bs, or confirm GPUDirect RDMA is actually active
(NCCL_DEBUG=INFO should show the IB/GDRDMA path; a silent fallback to a host-staged path is a common
and expensive failure mode).

Step 5 -- if the symptom is OOM rather than slowness: peak activation memory scales with in-flight
microbatches (~P under 1F1B), not with M, so raising M is memory-neutral while raising P is not.
Options in increasing order of cost: enable selective activation recomputation, reduce micro_bs,
rebalance layers off the hot stage, then raise P.

Step 6 -- change one variable, rerun with at least 20 warmup and 5 measured steps, report median and
p90, and keep the previous config in the job spec so rollback is a one-line revert.

Rollback gate: revert immediately if tokens/s regresses >3%, if any rank's peak memory exceeds 90% of
device memory, or if the loss curve leaves the established seed-noise band within 200 steps. Never
carry a config change past a checkpoint boundary without a comparison run.

Escalate instead of tuning blindly if NCCL_DEBUG shows a transport fallback, if per-stage times are
unstable run-to-run (suspect clock throttling or a noisy neighbor), or if the fabric reports
retransmits -- those are cluster faults, not tuning targets. (Case variant 1.)
